global.headline: TRUMP THREATENS TO BOMB OMAN AS 60-DAY MOU WINDOW LAPSES; IRAN CLAIMS HORMUZ DEAL WITH MUSCAT AS KHAMENEI'S SON DIGS IN FOR A LONG WAR
summary: The 60-day ceasefire-extension window set by the 17 June US-Iran memorandum of understanding expired Monday with the war no closer to resolution. In a Fox News phone interview, President Trump said Iran "should put up the white flag of surrender," claimed he faced no time pressure ("I'm not in a hurry"), and, asked about Oman's parallel mediation with Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, threatened: "If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the [expletive] out of them." Trump said the expired deadline was irrelevant since there is no fixed timeline to end the conflict.

Hours earlier, Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency said Tehran and Oman had reached agreement on a "shipping map" governing Hormuz traffic, with a joint statement in final drafting — an arrangement Iranian officials describe as bilateral and sovereignty-preserving, distinct from any deal with Washington. Trump's threat against Oman, the only state with a working channel to both sides, lands squarely on top of that announcement; the US has spent weeks pushing Muscat toward a free-transit outcome Iran has resisted. Separately, US intelligence cited by the Wall Street Journal suggests Iran's hardline leadership has spent the past two months preparing for the war to widen rather than end, citing communications between Iran and allied militias.

Iran's publicly reclusive Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in hiding since March, gave his clearest signal yet of his own posture this month by installing a string of hardline, veteran military commanders in top security roles and ordering the merger of the regular armed forces' general staff with the IRGC's Khatam ol-Anbia central headquarters — a move analysts say streamlines wartime IRGC-Artesh coordination and signals he is settling in for open-ended confrontation, not a near-term deal. Separately, bipartisan Senate criticism mounted over Trump's weekend order to scale back this week's US-South Korea drills after Seoul declined to help pressure Iran: Senate Armed Services ranking Democrat Jack Reed called it "another inane, haphazard decision," arguing it hands Kim Jong Un "a propaganda victory," while Republican Thom Tillis said it merely frees North Korean troops to keep supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
global.geopolitical: A US president publicly threatening to bomb the one Gulf state whose mediation channel with Iran is still functioning — even as that channel produces its first concrete Hormuz-management agreement of the war — risks souring the mediator Washington itself needs, while Khamenei's hardline security reshuffle and the bipartisan alarm over South Korea both point the same direction: a war approaching its seventh month with the actors on every side settling in rather than seeking exits.
global.socioeconomic: Oil barely moved on the bombing threat (Brent closed essentially flat around US$88/barrel) — a sign traders now discount this now-familiar pattern of rhetoric outpacing action — even as the underlying cost of the standoff keeps compounding: elevated Hormuz war-risk insurance, a US-South Korea alliance strain with its own economic and deterrence costs, and an Iran-Oman shipping arrangement that, absent a matching US concession, cannot by itself reopen the strait to normal traffic.

global.headline: ZAMBIA ARRESTS OPPOSITION FIGURES IN ELECTION-NIGHT RAID ON MUNDUBILE'S HOME AS VOTE COUNT PUTS HICHILEMA ON COURSE FOR OUTRIGHT WIN
summary: Zambia's government said a joint security operation on the night of 13 August at presidential candidate Brian Mundubile's Kabulonga residence in Lusaka uncovered a suspected militia cell in possession of "high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection," which it said had been under surveillance for months. The government said Mundubile was present when 11 people were apprehended and that shots were fired from the premises at law enforcement, triggering an exchange of fire; it named six people in custody, including a Mundubile spokesperson and what it called "senior members of certain political parties."

Mundubile, the New Revolutionary Republican Progressive United Party's presidential candidate and incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema's main challenger, denied any militia link and called the government's account "fabricated" to divert attention from the disputed vote count. The arrests land as the Electoral Commission of Zambia's count reached 161 of 226 constituencies, with Hichilema's vote share climbing to roughly 62% (867,066-vote lead) against Mundubile's 36% — a margin putting the incumbent on course for a first-round win without a run-off, and coming after SADC observers had already documented widespread election-period intimidation and violence.
global.geopolitical: Arresting a losing opposition candidate's inner circle on election night, whatever the underlying facts, hands international observers and Mundubile's supporters a ready-made narrative of a tilted process just as Hichilema closes in on the outright majority that would spare Zambia a contested run-off.
global.socioeconomic: A credibility cloud over the vote — layered on SADC's own documentation of assaults, intimidation and property damage during the count — raises the risk of prolonged post-election unrest and legal challenges that could unsettle investor confidence in a country whose economy has been steadily recovering under Hichilema's first term.

global.headline: ZIMBABWE FERRY DEATH TOLL RISES TO 84, DEADLIEST BOAT DISASTER IN THE COUNTRY'S HISTORY
summary: The death toll from the 11 August capsizing of the government-operated ferry Mbuya Nehanda on Lake Kariba rose to 84, including 18 children, after 12 more bodies were recovered over the weekend — up from 68 reported two days earlier and more than double the initial 44 confirmed in the disaster's first hours. It is now the deadliest boat disaster in Zimbabwe's history.

The vessel, operated by the state's Rural Infrastructure Development Agency on the Kariba-Chalala route, was authorised to carry 90 people but was carrying at least 114 adults plus five crew and an unspecified number of children — some estimates put the true count as high as 153. Seventy-seven people were rescued; recovery operations continued through the weekend as the toll climbed.
global.geopolitical: As a state-operated ferry service, the disaster puts direct pressure on Zimbabwe's government over transport-safety oversight, adding to the reputational costs Harare already carries over public-infrastructure standards.
global.socioeconomic: Lake Kariba's ferries are a lifeline for remote communities with few road alternatives, so any capacity crackdown in response risks disrupting the very travel and trade the service exists to enable — underscoring the tension between safety enforcement and transport access in Zimbabwe's rural economy.

global.headline: DR CONGO'S EBOLA OUTBREAK BECOMES DEADLIEST IN THE COUNTRY'S HISTORY, SURPASSING THE 2018-2020 RECORD
summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo's public health institute said Sunday that the Bundibugyo-strain Ebola outbreak, first detected in late April, had killed 2,325 people as of data through 15 August — surpassing the 2,299 deaths recorded in the 2018-2020 North Kivu/Ituri outbreak, previously the country's deadliest. Confirmed cases stand at 4,945, already the largest outbreak by case count in DRC's history (since late July) and the world's second-largest Ebola outbreak ever, behind only West Africa's 2014-2016 epidemic (28,616 cases, 11,310 deaths).

What distinguishes the current outbreak is speed: it reached 2,000 deaths within roughly three months of detection, though researchers say it may have been spreading undetected since February. No vaccine or treatment is approved for the Bundibugyo strain specifically — existing Ebola countermeasures target the more common Zaire ebolavirus species.
global.geopolitical: A record-breaking outbreak with no approved vaccine or treatment for its specific viral strain sharpens pressure on WHO and international donors to accelerate emergency countermeasure development and cross-border containment support, particularly given the outbreak's proximity to DRC's border regions.
global.socioeconomic: The scale and speed of the outbreak is straining an already fragile eastern DRC health system and displacing economic activity across affected provinces, with the absence of a strain-specific vaccine leaving containment reliant on slower, more resource-intensive measures like contact tracing and isolation.

global.headline: KUSHNER'S MARATHON GAZA TALKS WITH NETANYAHU END WITHOUT BREAKTHROUGH, A DAY AFTER RARE HAMAS MEETING
summary: US envoy Jared Kushner left Jerusalem on Monday without a breakthrough after an hours-long meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — also attended by former UK PM Tony Blair and Board of Peace director Nickolay Mladenov — that came a day after Kushner spent more than two hours meeting Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt on disarmament, a rare direct US-Hamas engagement.

The core dispute remains sequencing: Netanyahu and Kushner agreed Gaza's reconstruction will not begin until Hamas is fully disarmed, including of light weapons, while Hamas says it has already agreed to the 15-point US-backed road map and wants mediators to "compel" Israel to sign on. The two sides did agree to establish working groups on disarmament and on sanitation, clean water and other public health issues — concrete but modest steps. Officials described the outcome as moderately optimistic but with no firm Israeli commitment to the broader plan.
global.geopolitical: Washington's top Middle East negotiator spending consecutive days with both Hamas and Netanyahu, without resolving the fundamental disarm-first-versus-withdraw-first disagreement, shows real diplomatic urgency nearly three weeks after Hamas's own signature on the framework but underscores how far the two sides remain from an actual handoff.
global.socioeconomic: The new working group on sanitation, clean water and public health is a tangible, if narrow, step for a Gaza population still without reconstructed infrastructure, but the broader rebuilding effort — and the funding pledges tied to it — stays hostage to the unresolved disarmament sequencing.

singapore.headline: SECOND FAKE 'CONSULTANCY' CAUGHT TRYING TO RECRUIT FORMER SINGAPORE DIPLOMATS, ECHOING EARLIER INFOASSA CASE
summary: A CNA investigation identified an online entity called "Great Vision" whose website is trying to recruit former Singapore Ministry of Foreign Affairs personnel. The site falsely claims to be Singapore-headquartered and that its "managing partner" is a former Singapore diplomat — a claim CNA's checks found to be untrue.

The find extends the same fake-consultancy pattern CNA first exposed on 10 August with Infoassa, a Singapore-registered entity found to be using fabricated staff profiles and recruitment tactics echoing established foreign-intelligence tradecraft, including matching a website previously seized by US authorities over Chinese-intelligence links. Details on Great Vision's ownership or the extent of its recruitment activity remain limited pending further reporting.
singapore.geopolitical: A second fake-consultancy front targeting Singapore's foreign-policy alumni within weeks of the first suggests a sustained recruitment effort against the city-state's diplomatic and security community rather than an isolated incident, raising the stakes for MFA and RSIS to warn former personnel explicitly.
singapore.socioeconomic: Cases like this erode trust in Singapore's genuine, thriving think-tank and consultancy sector, forcing legitimate organisations to more actively verify their own credentials against a backdrop of fabricated look-alikes.

singapore.headline: COMPETITION WATCHDOG WARNS BIKE-SHARE FIRM HELLORIDE OVER ATTEMPTS TO FIX PRICES WITH RIVAL ANYWHEEL
summary: The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCS) warned Shanghai-headquartered bike-sharing operator HelloRide (trading as HelloBikeSG) after a representative twice — in July and October last year — approached homegrown rival Anywheel to propose price discussions, Singapore's only two licensed shared-bicycle operators. CCS said the conduct did not breach Section 34 of the Competition Act, since no commercially sensitive information was exchanged and Anywheel declined to engage, but warned that coordination between the market's only two licensees could significantly harm competition.
CCS commended Anywheel for rebuffing the approach and reporting it, which triggered the investigation, saying "Anywheel's conduct is what we expect of responsible market participants."
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic regulatory matter with no material international dimension.
singapore.socioeconomic: The warning reinforces CCS's enforcement posture in Singapore's small, duopoly-prone shared-mobility market, signalling to both operators — and to other tightly-held local markets — that even unsuccessful price-coordination overtures carry regulatory risk.

singapore.headline: PAP-WP CLASH OVER WORKERS' PARTY ECONOMIC MOTION SPILLS ONLINE AS EX-MINISTER OF STATE CALLS IT 'POLITICAL OPPORTUNISM'
summary: The debate over the Workers' Party's "economy of the future" parliamentary motion — tabled 3 August and passed in amended form after a nine-hour debate on 6 August — resurfaced online after former Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry and National Development Lee Yi Shyan wrote on Facebook (16 August) that he was "taken aback" by WP MP Kenneth Tiong's call for "an economic engine driven by dynamic local companies" and "healthy domestic demand," arguing Singapore's six-million-person domestic market cannot substitute for foreign investment and global markets, and describing what he called "a familiar pattern" of inconsistency in WP's policy positions.

Tiong rebutted Lee on Facebook Monday, saying Lee had mischaracterised WP's position as a zero-sum choice between local enterprise and multinationals: "What we suggested was to supercharge local enterprise: automatic support for new registrants, seconded experts, wider R&D tax deductions, grants to match MNC starting salaries, German-style internships. None of it, a zero-sum policy." Tiong added that WP had said domestic demand is "necessary, not sufficient," and rejected the suggestion that the party had backed down from its own motion.
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic political dispute with no material international dimension.
singapore.socioeconomic: The exchange keeps alive a live disagreement over Singapore's next-phase growth model — continued reliance on MNC-anchored FDI versus a deliberate tilt toward local-enterprise support — that will likely resurface as both parties position ahead of the next General Election.

singapore.headline: KALLANG DISTRIPARK SET FOR REDEVELOPMENT INTO THOUSANDS OF NEW PRIVATE HOMES
summary: The Kallang Distripark site is slated for redevelopment into private housing, part of a wider URA-backed vision under the Draft Master Plan 2025 to revive Kallang River waterfront sites — including Kallang Distripark, Kallang Industrial Estate and Tanjong Rhu — for thousands of new homes. Property analysts estimate Kallang Distripark alone could yield more than 2,000 new units. Part of the site is freehold while another part sits on a 99-year lease expiring in 2067; URA said the precise redevelopment timeline "will be reviewed in due time."
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic land-use and housing-supply matter with no material international dimension.
singapore.socioeconomic: A multi-thousand-unit addition along the Kallang River would meaningfully expand private housing supply in a well-connected central-fringe location, part of a broader government push to convert ageing industrial waterfront land into housing as land available for new towns grows scarcer.

word.etymology: From French gasconnade, from Gascon, a native of Gascony, France, stereotyped in French literature as boastful; entered English in the early 18th century.
word.example: Trump's vow to "bomb the [expletive] out of" Oman if it "gets in the way," delivered alongside a taunt that Iran should raise the "white flag of surrender" even as the war's own 60-day deadline quietly lapsed with no deal in hand, was pure gasconade dressed up as policy.
